title: Level 5 · Intermediate Python
blurb: Comprehensions, modules, error handling and working with files, JSON, CSV and regular expressions.

lessons.title: List Comprehension
lessons.concept: A list comprehension builds a new list in one line: [expression for item in items if condition]. It is a short form of a loop that appends to a list. The if part is optional and keeps only matching items.
lessons.why: Cleaning and transforming lists of data is a daily job, and comprehensions make it short and readable.
lessons.example:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print([n * 10 for n in nums])
print([n for n in nums if n % 2 == 1])
lessons.example_note: Multiplies every number by 10, then keeps only the odd ones.
lessons.prompt: Write squares_of_evens(nums) that returns a list of the squares of only the even numbers, using a list comprehension (no append).
lessons.solution:
def squares_of_evens(nums):
    return [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
hints: Shape: [what_to_keep for n in nums if condition].
Even means n % 2 == 0.
return [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]

lessons.title: Dictionary Comprehension
lessons.concept: A dictionary comprehension builds a dict in one line using curly braces and a key: value pair: {word: len(word) for word in words}. It works just like a list comprehension.
lessons.why: Turning a list into a lookup table, like name to score or product to price, is very common.
lessons.example:
fruits = ['apple', 'fig']
print({f: len(f) for f in fruits})
lessons.example_note: Maps each fruit to the length of its name.
lessons.prompt: Write name_lengths(names) that returns a dictionary mapping each name to its length, using a dictionary comprehension.
lessons.solution:
def name_lengths(names):
    return {name: len(name) for name in names}
hints: Curly braces with key: value, then for ... in names.
The key is the name, the value is len(name).
return {name: len(name) for name in names}

lessons.title: Set Comprehension
lessons.concept: A set comprehension looks like a dictionary one but with a single value: {x for x in items}. A set keeps each value only once, so duplicates disappear automatically.
lessons.why: Finding the unique cities, tags or first letters in a pile of data is a set job.
lessons.example:
words = ['apple', 'avocado', 'banana']
print(sorted({w[0] for w in words}))
lessons.example_note: Collects the unique first letters (sorted so the output is stable).
lessons.prompt: Write unique_first_letters(words) that returns a set of the lowercase first letters of the words, using a set comprehension.
lessons.solution:
def unique_first_letters(words):
    return {w[0].lower() for w in words}
hints: Use curly braces with one expression and a for.
w[0] is the first letter; .lower() makes it lowercase.
return {w[0].lower() for w in words}

lessons.title: Generator Expression
lessons.concept: A generator expression is a comprehension in round brackets: (x * x for x in range(5)). It does not build a list; it produces values one at a time when asked, which saves memory. Functions like sum() accept it directly: sum(x for x in nums).
lessons.why: When data is huge (millions of rows), a generator avoids storing everything at once.
lessons.example:
squares = (n * n for n in range(1, 4))
print(next(squares))
print(sum(n * n for n in range(1, 4)))
lessons.example_note: Takes one value from a generator, then sums another one.
lessons.prompt: Write sum_of_squares(n) that returns 1*1 + 2*2 + ... + n*n using sum() with a generator expression (do not build a list with square brackets).
lessons.solution:
def sum_of_squares(n):
    return sum(i * i for i in range(1, n + 1))
hints: range(1, n + 1) gives 1 up to n.
Pass the generator straight into sum(...).
return sum(i * i for i in range(1, n + 1))

lessons.title: Modules (import, custom modules)
lessons.concept: A module is a file of ready-made Python code. Load it with import math and use its tools as math.sqrt(16). Python ships with many (math, statistics, random). Your own file tools.py is also a module: import tools.
lessons.why: Modules let you reuse tested code instead of writing everything yourself, and keep big projects organised in files.
lessons.example:
import math
import statistics

print(math.sqrt(49))
print(statistics.mean([2, 4, 9]))
lessons.example_note: Imports two standard modules and uses one function from each.
lessons.prompt: Read one line of space-separated numbers. Import statistics and math, then print the mean on the first line and the mean rounded down (math.floor) on the second. Example: 10 20 30 prints 20.0 then 20.
lessons.starter:
# import statistics and math here

nums = [float(x) for x in input().split()]
# print the mean, then the floor of the mean
lessons.solution:
import statistics
import math

nums = [float(x) for x in input().split()]
mean = statistics.mean(nums)
print(mean)
print(math.floor(mean))
hints: Put import statistics and import math at the top.
statistics.mean(nums) gives the average.
Print the mean, then print(math.floor(mean)).

lessons.title: Packages
lessons.concept: A package is a folder of modules, with a file named __init__.py marking it as a package. Inside it modules can be grouped, e.g. shop/billing.py is imported as import shop.billing or from shop import billing. The standard library has packages too: os is a package and os.path is a module inside it.
lessons.why: Packages organise large projects into folders, and almost every third-party library you install is a package.
lessons.example_note: Uses the path module that lives inside the os package.
lessons.prompt: Use import os.path to write split_name(filename) that returns the result of os.path.splitext(filename): the name and the extension as a tuple.
lessons.starter:
# import os.path

def split_name(filename):
    # return os.path.splitext(filename)
    pass
hints: Put import os.path at the top of the file.
os.path.splitext splits at the last dot.
return os.path.splitext(filename)

lessons.title: Exception Handling (try, except, finally)
lessons.concept: An exception is an error that stops your program, like dividing by zero. Wrap risky code in try: and catch the problem with except ZeroDivisionError: so the program carries on. A finally: block runs at the end whether or not an error happened.
lessons.why: Real programs must survive bad input, missing files and network failures instead of crashing.
lessons.example_note: Catches the error, prints a friendly message, then runs finally.
lessons.prompt: Write safe_divide(a, b) that returns a / b, but returns the text 'Cannot divide by zero' when b is 0. Use try and except.
hints: Put the division inside try:
Catch it with except ZeroDivisionError:
try: return a / b  /  except ZeroDivisionError: return 'Cannot divide by zero'

lessons.title: Custom Exceptions (raise)
lessons.concept: You can signal your own errors with raise. Make a new error type by writing a class that inherits from Exception: class MyError(Exception): pass. Then raise MyError('message') stops the function, and callers can catch it with except MyError as e; str(e) is the message.
lessons.why: Custom errors give clear names to problems in your own rules, like InsufficientFunds in a banking app.
lessons.example_note: Raises a custom error and catches it, printing its message.
lessons.prompt: Create class InsufficientFunds(Exception). Write withdraw(balance, amount) that raises InsufficientFunds('Not enough money') if amount is more than balance, otherwise returns the new balance. The check helper is already written for you.
hints: class InsufficientFunds(Exception): with pass inside.
In withdraw, test amount > balance first.
raise InsufficientFunds('Not enough money') in that if; otherwise return balance - amount.

lessons.title: File Handling (read, write, append)
lessons.concept: Open a file with with open('name.txt', mode) as f:; the with closes it for you. Modes: 'r' read, 'w' write (erases old content), 'a' append (adds at the end). Use f.write(text) to write and f.read() to read it all back.
lessons.why: Saving notes, logs and results to disk lets data live after your program ends.
lessons.example:
with open('hello.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('Line one\n')
with open('hello.txt', 'a') as f:
    f.write('Line two\n')
with open('hello.txt') as f:
    print(f.read())
lessons.example_note: Writes a file, appends to it, then reads it back.
lessons.prompt: Write make_notes(first, second). It writes first and a newline into notes.txt (mode 'w'), appends second and a newline (mode 'a'), then reads the file and returns its lines as a list (splitlines()).
lessons.solution:
def make_notes(first, second):
    with open('notes.txt', 'w') as f:
        f.write(first + '\n')
    with open('notes.txt', 'a') as f:
        f.write(second + '\n')
    with open('notes.txt') as f:
        return f.read().splitlines()
hints: Use three with open(...) blocks: write, append, read.
Write with f.write(first + '\n') in mode 'w'.
Return f.read().splitlines() from the last block.

lessons.title: JSON Handling
lessons.concept: JSON is a text format for data that looks like Python dicts and lists. json.dumps(obj) turns an object into a JSON string and json.loads(text) turns it back. json.dump(obj, file) and json.load(file) do the same with open files.
lessons.why: Websites, apps and settings files all exchange data as JSON.
lessons.example:
import json

data = {'name': 'Asha', 'age': 20}
text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)
print(json.loads(text)['name'])
lessons.example_note: Converts a dict to a JSON string and reads a value back.
lessons.prompt: Write save_and_load(data): save data to data.json with json.dump, read it back with json.load, and return json.dumps(loaded, sort_keys=True).
lessons.starter:
import json

def save_and_load(data):
    # json.dump to a file, json.load it back, return json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True)
    pass
lessons.solution:
import json

def save_and_load(data):
    with open('data.json', 'w') as f:
        json.dump(data, f)
    with open('data.json') as f:
        loaded = json.load(f)
    return json.dumps(loaded, sort_keys=True)
hints: Open data.json with 'w' and call json.dump(data, f).
Open it again for reading and call json.load(f).
return json.dumps(loaded, sort_keys=True)

lessons.title: CSV Handling
lessons.concept: CSV files store tables as text, one row per line with values separated by commas. csv.reader(file) gives each row as a list of strings, and csv.writer(file) writes rows with writerow(). Any file-like object works, including io.StringIO(text), a file made from a string.
lessons.why: Spreadsheets and exported reports are CSV files, so reading them is a common data task.
lessons.example:
import csv
import io

text = 'item,price\npen,10\nbook,45'
for row in csv.reader(io.StringIO(text)):
    print(row)
lessons.example_note: Prints each row as a list of strings.
lessons.prompt: Write total_price(csv_text) that reads CSV text with a header row (item,price) using csv.reader and returns the sum of the prices as an integer.
lessons.starter:
import csv
import io

def total_price(csv_text):
    # reader = csv.reader(io.StringIO(csv_text)); skip the header with next(reader)
    pass
lessons.solution:
import csv
import io

def total_price(csv_text):
    reader = csv.reader(io.StringIO(csv_text))
    next(reader)
    total = 0
    for row in reader:
        total += int(row[1])
    return total
hints: Call next(reader) once to skip the header.
Each row is a list: row[1] is the price text, so use int().
Loop over reader, add int(row[1]) to a total and return it.

lessons.title: Regular Expressions (re module)
lessons.concept: A regular expression is a pattern for finding text. With import re, re.findall(pattern, text) returns all matches as a list. In patterns \d means a digit, + means one or more, so \d+ matches whole numbers. Write patterns as raw strings: r'\d+'.
lessons.why: Validating emails and phone numbers or pulling data out of messy text are classic regex jobs.
lessons.example:
import re

text = 'Order 12 has 3 items'
print(re.findall(r'\d+', text))
print(bool(re.search(r'items', text)))
lessons.example_note: Finds the numbers in a sentence, then checks a word is present.
lessons.prompt: Write extract_numbers(text) that returns a list of all the whole numbers (as strings) found in the text, using re.findall.
lessons.starter:
import re

def extract_numbers(text):
    # return re.findall(r'...', text)
    pass
hints: re.findall(pattern, text) returns a list of matches.
\d+ matches one or more digits.
return re.findall(r'\d+', text)
